articles.title: Fact or opinion?

body.support:
Reviews, ads and posts mix **facts** and **opinions**.

**A fact can be checked.** *The gym opens at 6am. It costs $25 a week.* You could check if it's true.

**An opinion is what someone thinks.** *It's the best gym. It's too expensive.* You can't prove it.

**Opinion words**

- *best, worst, amazing, terrible*
- *should, must*
- *I think, I reckon*
- *too, way too*.

**Mixed sentences.** *“The skate park cost $2 million, and it's a waste.”* The cost is a fact. *A waste* is an opinion.

**Opinions can help.** A review from someone who went there is useful. Just know it's an opinion.

**Find the main point.** What does the writer want you to think? What reasons do they give? Are they facts or opinions?

**Star ratings** are lots of opinions added up. They can be faked. Read the bad reviews too.
body.core:
Every day you read reviews, ads, posts and news that mix **facts** and **opinions**. Knowing which is which is one of the most useful reading skills there is.

**Facts can be checked.** A **fact** can be proved true or false. *The gym opens at 6am. Membership costs $25 a week. The council voted 6 to 3.* You might not know if it's true yet, but you could check.

**Opinions are what someone thinks.** An **opinion** is a feeling, belief or judgement. *It's the best gym in town. It's way too expensive. The council made the wrong call.* You can agree or disagree, but you can't prove it.

**Signal words.** Opinions often use words like:

- *best, worst, greatest, terrible, amazing, boring*
- *should, must, ought to*
- *I think, I believe, I reckon, in my view*
- *too, way too, much better*.

**Mixed sentences.** Lots of sentences have both. *“The new skate park cost $2 million, and it's a total waste.”* The cost is a fact. *Total waste* is an opinion.

**Opinions aren't bad.** A review from someone who's been there can be really useful. Expert opinions, like a doctor's advice, are worth listening to. Just know it's an opinion, and think about who's giving it and why.

**Finding the main argument.** Persuasive texts make a point, then back it up. Ask:

1. What does the writer want me to think or do? (That's the **main argument**.)
2. What **reasons** do they give?
3. Which reasons are **facts**, and which are **opinions**?
4. Can I **check** the facts?

**Reviews and stars.** A star rating is a lot of opinions added together. It can be useful. But reviews can be faked, paid for, or filtered so only the good ones show. Read a few of the worst ones too.
body.extend:
Reviews, advertisements, posts, news and speeches routinely combine **facts** and **opinions**. Distinguishing them is fundamental to critical reading.

**Facts are verifiable.** A **fact** can be proven true or false: *The gym opens at 6am. Membership is $25 a week. The council voted 6–3.* Even if you haven't checked it yet, it's checkable.

**Opinions are judgements.** An **opinion** expresses a belief, feeling or evaluation: *It's the best gym in town. It's overpriced. The council got it wrong.* It can be agreed or disagreed with, but not proven.

**Signal words.** Opinions are often marked by superlatives and evaluative adjectives (*best, worst, outstanding, appalling*), modal verbs (*should, must, ought to*), and stance markers (*I believe, in my view, clearly*).

**Mixed statements.** Many sentences combine both: *“The skate park cost $2 million, and it's a complete waste.”* The cost is factual; *complete waste* is evaluative.

**The value of opinion.** Opinions aren't inherently unreliable. Informed opinion, such as an expert's assessment or a customer's first-hand experience, can be valuable. The key is recognising it as opinion and considering who holds it and why.

**Main ideas and arguments.** Persuasive texts advance a **main argument** supported by reasons. Identify the argument, separate factual reasons from opinions, and **verify** the facts.

**Aggregated opinion.** Star ratings combine many opinions. They can be informative, but reviews can be fabricated, incentivised or selectively filtered. Read critical reviews as well as glowing ones.

caseStudies.title: The reviews that went missing

body.support:
Reviews are **opinions**. Lots of reviews together can help you choose.

**Meriton** is a big company that rents out apartments. TripAdvisor emailed guests after their stay, asking them to write a review.

But in **2014 and 2015**, Meriton stopped some unhappy guests from getting those emails. So fewer bad reviews appeared.

The **ACCC** took Meriton to court. In **2018**, Meriton had to pay **$3 million**.

The lesson: each review was real. But someone chose which ones you saw. Always read some bad reviews too.
body.core:
When you book a hotel or apartment, you probably check the reviews. Reviews are **opinions**. But when you put lots of them together, they can tell you a lot. Unless someone is choosing which opinions get heard.

**Meriton** is a big Australian property company. It runs serviced apartments. For a time, it used a TripAdvisor service that emailed guests after their stay, inviting them to write a review.

But from **November 2014 to October 2015**, Meriton changed some guests' email addresses before sending them to TripAdvisor. These were guests it thought might leave a bad review. Because their addresses were changed, they never got the invitation. So fewer negative reviews appeared.

The **ACCC** (the government body that protects consumers) took Meriton to court. In **2017**, the **Federal Court** found Meriton had misled the public. In **July 2018**, the court ordered Meriton to pay **$3 million** in penalties.

The lesson: each review was a real opinion. But the **overall picture** was not a fair fact. When you read reviews, look at the bad ones too. And remember that someone may be controlling which opinions you see.
body.extend:
Each online review is one person's **opinion**. Added together, reviews shape what people decide. But that only works if the reviews are a fair sample.

**Meriton** is a major Australian property group. It used a TripAdvisor service that emailed guests after their stay, inviting them to write a review.

Between **November 2014 and October 2015**, Meriton changed ("masked") the email addresses of guests it thought would leave bad reviews. TripAdvisor's invitations never reached them. So fewer critical reviews were posted.

The **ACCC** took Meriton to court. In **2017**, the **Federal Court** found that Meriton had misled the public. In **July 2018**, the court ordered it to pay **$3 million** in penalties.

The case shows a subtle point. Every review that was posted was a genuine opinion. But the overall rating, which looked like a fair picture, had been skewed by filtering. Good readers think about what opinions say, and also about which opinions they are being shown, and by whom.

teacher.overview: Students learn to distinguish facts (checkable) from opinions (judgements), recognise opinion signal words, split mixed sentences, and identify the main argument and reasons in persuasive texts such as reviews, ads and posts. They annotate a made-up gym review, sort sentences, split mixed statements, and pull apart a real review, checking two facts. The case study is Meriton: from November 2014 to October 2015 it masked the emails of guests likely to leave negative reviews so they didn't receive TripAdvisor invitations; in July 2018 the Federal Court ordered it to pay $3 million.
prep: Find two or three real reviews (local business, game, film) to model.
Optional: the ACCC's consumer guidance on online reviews.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** facts can be checked; opinions are judgements (e.g. opens at 6am / best gym). E.g. best, worst, should, I think. What does the writer want me to think? What reasons? Facts or opinions? Can I check the facts?

**Review:** 1 opinion; 2 fact; 3 opinion; 4 both; 5 fact claim (one experience); 6 opinion.

**Sort:** five colours — fact; most beautiful beach — opinion; $90 and terrible — both; council approved — fact; vote at 16 — opinion; favourite pie, 2,000 stores — both.

**Split:** sold out in ten minutes / best band ever · TAFE courses start in February / way better than uni · train 15 minutes late / system is a joke · no petrol costs / everyone should buy one.

**Case study:** each review was an opinion; the overall rating was presented as fair but was filtered; to protect bookings and reputation; read negative reviews, check dates, look across platforms.

realityCheck: **Students may say everything is an opinion.** Push back with checkable examples: times, prices, dates.
**Personal experience is tricky.** “I waited 20 minutes” is a claim about a fact, but only the writer can know it. Good discussion point.
**Use reviews students care about.** Games, sneakers, food.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Quick wins, and students use it straight away.
